name: Consciousness, coma and brain death
summary: Consciousness has two components, arousal, maintained by the ascending reticular activating system of the upper brainstem, hypothalamus and thalamus, and awareness, generated by the cerebral cortex and its thalamic connections, and impaired consciousness follows from a lesion of the paramedian upper brainstem, from bilateral thalamic or diffuse hemispheric dysfunction, or from a unilateral mass that compresses the brainstem by herniation. The examination of the comatose patient reads the brainstem level by level through the pupils, eye movements, corneal and gag reflexes, motor responses and breathing pattern, separates structural from metabolic coma, detects herniation in time to act, distinguishes coma from the locked-in state, the vegetative and minimally conscious states and psychogenic unresponsiveness, and, when all brainstem function is irreversibly lost, establishes brain death.

sections.heading: The anatomy of arousal
sections.body: Cholinergic, monoaminergic and glutamatergic neurons of the pontine and midbrain tegmentum project through the intralaminar thalamus and directly to the cortex and, with the orexin and histamine systems of the hypothalamus and the basal forebrain, keep the cortex awake; a lesion of the paramedian midbrain and upper pons, of both thalami, or of both hemispheres (diffuse injury, metabolic encephalopathy, drugs, seizures) produces coma, whereas a lesion of one hemisphere does so only by herniating. Awareness requires the cortex and its thalamocortical loops: the vegetative state (unresponsive wakefulness) has an intact brainstem with sleep-wake cycles, open eyes and reflex movements but no awareness after diffuse cortical or thalamic damage; the minimally conscious state shows inconsistent but reproducible signs of awareness; and the locked-in state, from a ventral pontine lesion, has full awareness with only vertical eye movements and blinking, and must never be mistaken for coma.

sections.heading: The examination of the comatose patient
sections.body: The level of consciousness is graded (Glasgow Coma Scale or FOUR score) and the brainstem is examined from top to bottom: pupils (equal and reactive in metabolic coma; a unilateral fixed dilated pupil in uncal herniation; midposition fixed in midbrain damage; pinpoint reactive in pontine damage or opioids; large and fixed in anticholinergic poisoning or death), eye position and the oculocephalic and caloric responses (intact in metabolic coma, absent with pontine damage, dysconjugate with brainstem lesions), corneal reflexes (pons), gag and cough (medulla), the motor response to pain (localizing, withdrawal, decorticate flexion from lesions above the red nucleus, decerebrate extension from midbrain-pontine lesions, none) and the breathing pattern (Cheyne-Stokes with bilateral hemispheric or diencephalic dysfunction, central hyperventilation with midbrain, apneustic and ataxic breathing with pontomedullary damage). Asymmetry means a structural lesion; preserved brainstem reflexes with deep coma mean a metabolic or toxic cause; and fundoscopy, neck stiffness and a skin and breath examination add the systemic clues.

sections.heading: Herniation and the rostrocaudal march
sections.body: A supratentorial mass raises pressure and displaces the brain: subfalcine herniation of the cingulate gyrus compresses the anterior cerebral artery; uncal herniation compresses the third nerve (dilated pupil), the posterior cerebral artery and the midbrain (contralateral then ipsilateral hemiplegia through Kernohan's notch), and central transtentorial herniation pushes the diencephalon and brainstem downward in a sequence of diencephalic (small reactive pupils, Cheyne-Stokes, decorticate posturing), midbrain (midposition fixed pupils, decerebrate posturing, hyperventilation), pontine (pinpoint pupils, absent oculocephalics, ataxic breathing) and medullary (apnea, cardiovascular collapse) stages; a posterior fossa mass produces upward or tonsillar herniation with medullary compression, apnea and death. Recognizing the stage, treating pressure (head elevation, osmotherapy, hyperventilation briefly, ventricular drainage, decompressive surgery) and removing the mass before the midbrain stage is the emergency of neurology.

sections.heading: Prognosis, disorders of consciousness and brain death
sections.body: After cardiac arrest, absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at 72 hours, absent cortical somatosensory evoked potentials, a malignant EEG, high neuron-specific enolase and diffuse cortical and basal ganglia diffusion change predict a poor outcome; after traumatic and other causes the trajectory is less certain and the vegetative state can evolve to minimal consciousness over months, so decisions are staged and functional imaging and careful behavioral scales are used. Brain death is the irreversible loss of all brainstem function: a known irreversible cause, no confounding drugs, hypothermia or metabolic derangement, deep coma with absent pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, caloric, gag and cough reflexes, no motor response of cranial nerve origin, and apnea on a formal test; ancillary tests (EEG, angiography, perfusion scintigraphy) support the diagnosis when the examination is incomplete. Spinal reflexes and the Lazarus sign can persist and do not contradict it.

keyPoints: Coma needs the paramedian upper brainstem, both thalami or both hemispheres; one hemisphere causes coma only by herniation
Reactive pupils with deep coma mean metabolic or toxic; an asymmetric or fixed pupil means structural
Decorticate flexion is above the red nucleus, decerebrate extension below it; the change marks the march of herniation
Locked-in patients are awake: ask for a blink or an upward gaze before calling anyone comatose
Brain death is a clinical diagnosis of the brainstem, made only when the cause is known and the confounders excluded
pearls: Examine the pupils every fifteen minutes in a patient with a mass: the pupil warns before the breathing stops
Naloxone, glucose and thiamine cost nothing and reverse three comas that look structural
The Glasgow score records the level; the brainstem reflexes record the site
pitfalls: Non-convulsive status epilepticus is a common unrecognized cause of coma with a normal CT; the EEG is part of the coma examination
A patient with a ventral pontine stroke who does not move is locked in, not unconscious, until proved otherwise

imaging.normalAppearance: CT identifies mass lesions, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus and the cisternal effacement of herniation; MRI with DWI shows diffuse hypoxic injury, brainstem lesions and the paramedian thalamic infarcts of Percheron; EEG separates non-convulsive status and encephalopathy; perfusion studies support brain death.

pathology.finding: Effacement of the suprasellar and perimesencephalic cisterns, medial temporal displacement over the tentorial edge, midline shift and later Duret hemorrhages in the brainstem.
Bilateral cortical ribbon, basal ganglia, thalamic and hippocampal restricted diffusion with loss of gray-white differentiation on CT after cardiac arrest.
Bilateral medial thalamic restricted diffusion with or without a midbrain lesion in a patient with sudden coma or hypersomnolence.
Absent intracranial arterial filling with opacification of the external carotid branches; radionuclide perfusion shows the hollow skull sign.
